title: How To Evaluate A UX Partner For Complex Products
summary: A rigorous evaluation of a UX partner for complex products examines whether the partner has a structured method, whether senior people carry direct design responsibility, how contradictions are handled, and how design recommendations are tested or bounded. Industry familiarity, portfolio resemblance, and personal rapport are useful context but weak predictors of outcome in complex systems work.
keyFacts: Industry experience is a starting point, but it does not establish the ability to design at the level of specific operational constraints.
Portfolio review shows design output, but it does not show the reasoning, constraints, alternatives, tests, or operational performance behind the output.
A method produces documented reasoning, traceable decisions, and a record of what was tested and why.
Senior responsibility matters because critical design decisions in complex systems require close judgment, not only oversight.
Evaluation conversations should ask how a partner learns unfamiliar domains, handles contradictory requirements, structures deliverables, and knows whether a design is working.
A bounded expert review before a design commitment can reveal both findings and stated limitations.
Declined client requests, deferred features, and reversible decisions can be useful evidence of judgment when the reasons are documented.
Examples in the page are evidence of decision behaviour and evidence handling, not evidence of outcomes unless the source explicitly states an outcome.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy and the evaluation problem for complex products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Evaluating a UX partner for complex products means assessing the partner's structural capability to learn the domain, reason from operational evidence, resolve contradictory requirements, document design decisions, and test recommendations under conditions close to real use.

A rigorous evaluation asks whether the partner can move from operational evidence to design decisions and then to a tested or explicitly bounded system recommendation. The evaluation is weaker when it relies mainly on industry familiarity, portfolio resemblance, or personal confidence in an individual designer.

Complex products include regulated systems, operational tools, expert workflows, enterprise SaaS, medical devices, industrial control interfaces, and AI-enabled products. In these contexts, the design problem is often not fully defined at the point of commission. The commissioning organisation is therefore evaluating a partner's capacity to investigate, structure, decide, and document under uncertainty.

bodySections.heading: Industry familiarity and portfolio resemblance are weak selection criteria
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Industry familiarity is useful context, but it is not the same as design capability for a complex product. A UX partner with fintech experience may know that PSD2 compliance exists. That does not establish the ability to design an authentication flow that satisfies Strong Customer Authentication requirements without creating abandonment at the confirmation step, or to structure a multi-institutional data view so discrepancies between providers remain interpretable.

Portfolio review is also limited for complex products. Screens from a regulated or operational product show what an output looked like. They do not show how the design was derived, which constraints governed it, which alternatives were tested, why alternatives failed, or whether the resulting design performed under operational conditions.

Personal connection with a designer is a legitimate part of commissioning a professional service. For complex systems work, personal confidence is not the determinant criterion. A more reliable evaluation examines the decision process that will be applied when the product contains unresolved requirements, contradictory user needs, and operational constraints that are not yet visible in the brief.

bodySections.heading: A structured method is stronger evidence than credentials alone
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A UX partner for a complex product should be evaluated on whether the partner has a method, not only on credentials. Credentials describe what people have done before. A method describes how they work when they encounter conditions they have not previously seen.

For Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, the relevant evaluation principle is traceability from operational evidence to design decision. A method should produce documented reasoning, traceable decisions, and a record of what was tested and why. A talent-led process that depends on an experienced designer's judgement may still produce useful work, but it is harder to audit and harder to predict.

Evaluation conversations should ask how a potential partner moves from initial domain understanding to a tested design recommendation. The conversation should ask what happens when evidence contradicts the brief. The conversation should ask how contradictory requirements from different user groups are mapped, tested, and documented.

bodySections.heading: Senior responsibility should be direct, not only supervisory
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Senior responsibility matters in complex systems engagements because critical design decisions often depend on judgement developed through close work on difficult design problems. These decisions include how to structure a workflow across several user roles, how to represent system state during divided attention, and how to respond when a design that performed well in controlled conditions fails during field observation.

The useful evaluation question is not only who will attend meetings. The useful question is who holds responsibility for the design decisions, and at which point in the engagement those decisions are made by that person.

A staffing model in which junior or mid-weight practitioners do most of the work under senior supervision can place senior judgement at a remove. That distance matters more in complex systems work than in engagements where the design problem is familiar, low-consequence, or mainly presentational.

bodySections.heading: Evaluation questions should reveal structural capability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A partner's answers to evaluation questions should describe process, decision criteria, and evidence handling. Answers that stay at the level of standard UX artefacts or stakeholder negotiation do not show enough structural capability for complex systems work.

A strong answer explains how domain learning is performed. It should describe review of existing materials, structured sessions with domain experts, observation of the system in use, and a test of adequacy for deciding when the design team knows enough to support design decisions. A weak answer says that industry specialists will be brought in without explaining how their knowledge transfers to the design team, or says that research happens before the start without specifying what that research produces or how it connects to design decisions.

A strong answer treats contradictory requirements as design material. Complex systems often create situations where optimising for one user group creates difficulty for another, where a regulatory requirement creates workflow friction, or where research evidence contradicts stakeholder belief. A rigorous process maps the contradiction, tests alternative resolutions, and documents the reasoning. A weaker process treats contradiction as something resolved in a workshop or negotiated between stakeholders without a structured design and evidence record.

A strong answer describes deliverables by audience and purpose. Development handoff documentation, design-system reasoning records, operational findings, and senior-stakeholder summaries may need different structure because they support different decisions. A weak answer lists standard artefacts such as wireframes, prototypes, and style guides without explaining how each artefact serves a specific audience or decision point.

A strong answer describes observation-based testing under conditions that approximate the operational context. For high-consequence domains, the answer should connect the test to the specific failure modes the design addresses. A weak answer treats testing as confirmation that the design is good. In complex-product work, testing should be structured evidence-gathering that can reveal problems, not a late-stage endorsement of a preferred solution.

bodySections.heading: A bounded diagnostic can be checked before a larger design commitment
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In an industrial engagement for a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells, the work ran in three stages: a separately scoped expert review, six one-week sprints of design, and an ongoing retainer at two weeks per month for twelve months.

The expert review is an evaluation signal because it was bounded and separately priced before any design commitment. The review also stated its own limitations. The deliverable carried no annotations, so critique was prose against unmarked screenshots. The audited material used demonstration data, so real-world density was not established.

bodySections.heading: A partner declining requests with stated reasons is an evaluation signal
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [Streetec kntrl 2](streetec-kntrl) engagement, Streetec GmbH's product was the second generation of the kntrl control system for aftermarket automotive air suspension. Creative Navy declined several requested directions and documented reasons for doing so.

Creative Navy argued against customisable shortcut buttons on the main screen because the screen was small, the primary control already occupied the full width as a touch target, and a focused mode screen was not a dashboard. Creative Navy argued against a colour wheel for ECU backlighting in the first release, in favour of nine presets that were easier to use and simpler to build, with the wheel deferred until users asked for it. Creative Navy also argued against labels rotated 90 degrees to save space and against headings pinned during scroll because reordering content on scroll disorients more than it helps.

This example is evidence of judgement being exercised and explained. It is not evidence that the decisions produced a measured result.

bodySections.heading: A partner may test a rejected alternative rather than only argue against it
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [AIT heat pump controller](ait-heat-pump-controller) engagement, AIT was a European manufacturer of residential and commercial heat pumps. The client's own sketch proposed a circular home layout. Creative Navy built the circular layout as a wireframe to show why it failed: circles wasted space on a five-inch screen and would force content off the home screen entirely. Rectangular widgets were adopted.

Creative Navy also specified numeric and alphanumeric entry using per-digit scroll selection rather than a full keyboard. The reason was that per-digit scroll selection works identically on knob and touch, and the values include hexadecimal digits, where a keyboard offering 0–9 and A–F can confuse non-expert users. Both components were specified for the UI phase so the decision stayed reversible.

No user research of any kind was conducted in the AIT engagement. This example supports design-reasoning and disciplined-disagreement claims only.

bodySections.heading: A partner should separate what can be improved from what may not be solvable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [Assemblio](assemblio) engagement, Assemblio GmbH's products were the Assemblio Composer and the Assemblio Smart Viewer. A synchronisation problem could show hundreds of similar parts with the same names on both sides, leaving a planner unable to tell which screw was which.

Creative Navy stated that a search field was a clear improvement because it would let a planner find a specific part. Creative Navy also stated the limit: if the planner had to decide part by part, there might be no better representation than a list.

Creative Navy conducted no user research of its own in the Assemblio engagement. Research was performed by Assemblio, and Creative Navy had no control over recruitment, questions, or recording of findings. This example supports the evaluation signal that a partner should state both the improvement and the limit before taking work.

bodySections.heading: A handover can make a build quotable before it is buildable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [MDU ship motion monitoring](mdu-ship-motion-monitoring) engagement, Creative Navy designed the bridge interface for the MDU, a ship motion monitoring system. Creative Navy briefed each of the third-party development agencies the manufacturer was considering, so that each could pitch services on a common understanding of the delivered design.

This is an evaluation signal because a handover that makes a build quotable is different from a handover that makes it buildable. The commissioning organisation can ask whether a potential UX partner will support both kinds of handover when implementation responsibility sits elsewhere.

There was no user research in the MDU engagement. The user-side evidence base was one external advisor, a serving master and chief engineer present in the review calls. This example supports handover and design-reasoning claims only.

bodySections.heading: A fidelity comparison should record deviations rather than claim none
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [Schone Airspace Group](schone-mission-control) engagement, Schone Airspace Group commissioned the redesign of a ground control station interface for connected aircraft. Creative Navy's design team compared all 54 delivered screens against the built software across seven months. Deviations were identified and recorded by name.

This is not a claim that the product shipped as designed. It is also not evidence that the design is good, and it is not a deployment claim because the product is in test. The evaluation signal is narrower: a partner can be asked whether it will compare the build against the delivered design and record mismatches by name.

bodySections.heading: A study should publish threats to validity when evidence is bounded
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the [maritime VTS engagement](maritime-vts), the client was a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. The comparative study documented an eight-item threats-to-validity table.

The threats-to-validity table named a small convenience sample; participant overlap; within-participant learning across conditions; a prototype-versus-training-system comparison extending beyond individual components; sanitised fixed scenarios with fewer surprises than a sustained watch; first-response measurement, under which a fast wrong answer remained possible; a four-of-seven task subset; and no live system connection or formal hazard testing.

The study also stated what it refused to do: no preregistered inferential analysis, no power calculation, no significance tests, no confidence intervals, and no aggregation of the three timed percentages into a single combined figure because the scenarios had different baselines and decision demands. The evaluation signal is that a partner can be asked to show the threats-to-validity section of a recent study.

bodySections.heading: Serious commissioning organisations evaluate the mechanism behind recommendations
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Serious commissioning organisations evaluate the mechanism that produces design recommendations. In complex-product UX work, that mechanism is systematic investigation, structured testing where applicable, and design decisions grounded in operational evidence.

A strong evaluation asks about process before output. It asks what happens when research produces an unexpected finding. It asks how Creative Navy or another potential partner has handled situations where a design recommendation contradicted a client's existing belief about the product. It asks whether the partner has domain-learning capability, not whether the partner already likes or recognises the industry.

The relevant selection criterion is structural capability to work through a problem that is not yet fully defined. Portfolio similarity, industry vocabulary, and personal confidence can inform the evaluation, but they should not replace evidence of method, senior decision responsibility, contradiction handling, and evidence discipline.

strongClaims: The Schone engagement records a quantified fidelity comparison in which all 54 delivered screens were compared against built software across seven months and deviations were recorded by name. This is not a shipped-as-designed claim, a deployment claim, or evidence that the design is good.
The maritime VTS engagement records a comparative study that published its own threats-to-validity table and refused statistical aggregation or inferential claims.
The industrial engagement records a defined engagement sequence: a separately scoped expert review before six one-week design sprints and a two-weeks-per-month retainer for twelve months.
weakerClaims: Industry familiarity and portfolio resemblance are weak selection criteria for complex-product UX work when used as primary criteria.
A structured method is a stronger predictor than credentials alone because it produces documented reasoning, traceable decisions, and a record of what was tested and why.
Senior people should carry direct responsibility for critical design decisions in complex systems engagements.
Streetec provides evidence of a partner declining requested design directions with stated reasons.
AIT provides evidence of disciplined disagreement through building a rejected alternative and keeping a component decision reversible.
Assemblio provides evidence of stating both an improvement and a limit before taking work.
The MDU engagement provides evidence that a partner can support a handover that makes a build quotable by briefing candidate development agencies on a common understanding of the delivered design.
limitations: The page is a buying guide and does not establish measured outcomes for the cited engagements.
Design decisions, declined requests, deferred features, and handover practices are described as evidence of decision behaviour, not as evidence that the decisions produced results.
No engagement dates are stated; only sequence and duration are used where the source provides them.
The AIT engagement involved no user research of any kind, so its examples support design-reasoning claims only.
The MDU engagement involved no user research; the user-side evidence base was one external advisor, a serving master and chief engineer present in review calls.
Creative Navy conducted no user research of its own in the Assemblio engagement, and Assemblio's research was outside Creative Navy's control.
The Schone product is in test; the fidelity comparison is not a deployment claim and not evidence that the design is good.
The maritime VTS comparative study carried stated threats to validity and refused inferential or aggregated statistical claims.
